title: CancellationToken design
description: Design cooperative cancellation patterns with CancellationToken, linked tokens, and timeout strategies.

data.text: Cancellation in .NET is cooperative: the caller signals that work should stop, and the callee checks the signal and exits gracefully. The `CancellationToken` struct is the standard way to pass this signal through your application.

A `CancellationToken` is created from a `CancellationTokenSource`. The source controls when cancellation is requested. The token is passed to methods that should respond to cancellation. Multiple tokens can be linked so that cancellation of any one source cancels the combined token.

data.title: Basic cancellation pattern

data.text: You often combine cancellation from multiple sources. A timeout and a user-initiated cancel should both stop the same operation. `CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource` merges two tokens into one.

data.title: Linked tokens: timeout + user cancel

items: Always pass `CancellationToken` as the last parameter.
Check `ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` in loops and before expensive steps.
Pass the token to I/O APIs (`HttpClient`, `Stream.ReadAsync`, EF Core queries).
Use linked tokens to combine timeout, user action, and parent cancellation.
Do not cancel a `CancellationTokenSource` while its token is still in use without disposing it.

data.title: Register callback carefully
data.text: `CancellationToken.Register` runs a callback when cancellation is requested. Avoid capturing variables that could be disposed or mutated unexpectedly. Use `CancellationToken` with `ConfigureAwait(false)` in library code to prevent context capture issues.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Cancellation is cooperative — the callee must check the token.
Link tokens when combining multiple cancellation sources.
Distinguish timeout cancellations from user cancellations.
